implementation_notes: .NET splits the control bus into two native halves. Status is instrumentation: a System.Diagnostics.Metrics Meter with counters and histograms, exported by OpenTelemetry or read live with dotnet-counters, plus DiagnosticSource/EventSource for events. Control is the host lifecycle and the admin surface: IHostApplicationLifetime (ApplicationStopping/StopApplication) and the CancellationToken handed to BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync request graceful shutdown, while commands become endpoints registered with MapHealthChecks/MapPost and protected with RequireAuthorization and RequireHost. Health-check middleware plus IHealthCheck is the standard watchdog surface, and configuration reload (IOptionsMonitor/ReloadOnChange) removes the need for many commands entirely. A message-based control bus is only justified when components cannot be addressed over HTTP or the operator already owns a broker.
pitfalls: StopApplication is a request, not an exit: code that assumes the process is gone immediately races the ApplicationStopping callbacks that still have to drain work.
MapHealthChecks and custom admin endpoints are a privileged control surface; without RequireAuthorization/RequireHost they are reachable from every interface the app listens on.
A BackgroundService that ignores the CancellationToken passed to ExecuteAsync keeps running after a stop command and makes the component report 'stopped' while it still consumes work.

variants.name: SignalR hub as the control channel for client-side components
variants.idiom_name: SignalR Hub<IControlClient> with command RPCs and status callbacks
variants.implementation_notes: Where the managed components are web clients rather than servers (edge gateways, browser-attached services, agents behind NAT), a SignalR hub makes a natural control channel: the console calls hub methods to send commands to a client, a group or everyone, and components push status back through the strongly typed Hub<T> interface, with SignalR handling transport fallback (WebSockets, server-sent events, long polling) and connection management. The hub is a privileged surface and must live on its own path with its own authentication scheme and authorisation policy. This variant complements the diagnostics/health variant: SignalR carries the commands, System.Diagnostics.Metrics still carries the telemetry.
pitfalls: Hub methods are callable by any client that can reach the hub: without an authentication scheme and an authorisation policy (and a hub separate from user-facing ones) the control bus is public.
SignalR reconnects and drops connections by design and does not guarantee delivery, so lifecycle commands must be acknowledged by the client and retried, never fired once.
Status callbacks are pushed by the component, so a component that stops sending status looks healthy unless the console tracks missed heartbeats and raises an alert.
